name: Amazonbot Checker
title: Amazonbot: Check If Amazon's Crawler Can Reach You
description: What is Amazonbot and should you allow it? Check your robots.txt and a live request as Amazonbot, plus what Amazon says it uses the crawler for.
answer: Amazonbot is Amazon's web crawler; Amazon says it improves its products and services and may be used to train Amazon AI models. A separate bot, Amzn-SearchBot, makes pages eligible for Alexa and Amazon search answers. Enter your site to see what robots.txt and your server allow each one.

body:
## What is Amazonbot used for?

Amazon now documents three agents, each controlled separately in robots.txt ([Amazon](https://developer.amazon.com/amazonbot)):

| Agent | What Amazon says it does | AI training? |
|---|---|---|
| Amazonbot | Improves Amazon products and services | May be used to train Amazon AI models |
| Amzn-SearchBot | Makes content eligible for search experiences such as Alexa | No |
| Amzn-User | Fetches live pages when a user asks Alexa something | No; may not follow every robots.txt rule |

Amazon adds two practical details: changes can take about 24 hours to apply, and its crawlers don't support the crawl-delay directive.

## Should I block Amazonbot?

Decide on the two main bots separately. Blocking Amazonbot opts you out of a crawler that may feed Amazon's AI training; blocking Amzn-SearchBot removes you from answers in Alexa and Amazon's search experiences.

For most brands, allowing Amzn-SearchBot is the easy call — it's a visibility bot with no training use. Amazonbot is the same kind of training decision as GPTBot or ClaudeBot.

## What do real sites do?

When we checked the robots.txt files of 391 well-known sites in October 2026 ([dataset](/resources/robots-agents-2026-10.json)), 9.4% blocked Amazonbot — 60.5% of news publishers, but only 1.6% of SaaS companies.

The newer bot is barely on anyone's radar: only 2.6% of robots.txt files named Amzn-SearchBot at all, and 3.4% blocked it, mostly through broad rules aimed at every bot.

## Does Amzn-SearchBot follow my other rules?

Partly. Amazon says that if robots.txt doesn't mention Amzn-SearchBot but allows other search bots, Amzn-SearchBot follows the directives given to those search bots. Naming it explicitly removes the guesswork.

Standard matching still applies: the most specific user-agent group wins ([RFC 9309](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html)), and Amazon reads robots.txt per host — `shop.example.com` needs its own file.

## What rules should I copy?

To stay in Alexa answers but opt out of training:

```
User-agent: Amazonbot
Disallow: /

User-agent: Amzn-SearchBot
Allow: /
```

Amazon also honors page-level robots meta tags: `noarchive` (don't use the page for model training), `noindex` and `none`. Check every AI bot at once with the [AI crawler checker](/tools/ai-crawlers), or build a full policy with the [AI robots.txt generator](/tools/ai-robots-txt-generator).

faqs.q: Is Amazonbot used for AI training?
faqs.a: Amazon says Amazonbot may be used to train Amazon AI models. Its other two agents, Amzn-SearchBot and Amzn-User, are documented as not crawling content for generative AI training.

faqs.q: Does blocking Amazonbot remove me from Alexa?
faqs.a: Not by itself. Alexa and Amazon search answers depend on Amzn-SearchBot, which has its own robots.txt group. Block Amazonbot and allow Amzn-SearchBot to keep that visibility.
No. Amazon says its crawlers do not support the crawl-delay directive. To reduce load, use robots.txt rules, rate limiting on your server, or contact Amazon at the address it publishes.
